title: Build a simple kite from a bag and two sticks
description: A plastic bag, two light sticks, string and tape: a diamond kite you can build on the kitchen table in half an hour and fly the same afternoon — plus why the tail is not decoration.

body.heading: Build the diamond
paragraphs: Cut a large plastic bag open into one flat sheet. Lay two light sticks — garden canes or wooden skewers taped together — in a cross on the sheet, the upright one longer than the sideways one, and tape the ends firmly. Cut the sheet into a diamond around the cross, fold the edges over the sticks, and tape them down so the frame cannot slip.

Tie your flying line to the point where the sticks cross, slightly above the middle. That attachment point, the bridle point, is where the kite balances against the wind — a centimetre up or down changes how it flies, and adjusting it is the whole craft of kite-making in miniature.

body.heading: The tail is not decoration
paragraphs: Cut a tail from strips of bag or ribbon, at least as long as the kite is tall, and tie small bows or knots along it. A new builder's kite that spins and dives is almost never broken — it is under-tailed. The tail adds drag behind the kite, which holds its nose into the wind the way feathers hold an arrow straight.

Fly in an open space away from trees, roads and power lines, on a steady breeze rather than a gusty day. If the kite loops, land it and lengthen the tail; if it will not climb, shorten it a little. You are now doing what kite builders have done for two thousand years: tuning by flying.

takeaway: A bag, two sticks and string make a working diamond kite — and its tail is real engineering: drag that holds the kite's nose into the wind, lengthened or shortened to tune the flight.
materials: Two light sticks or garden canes
String or light line for flying
Strips of bag or ribbon for the tail
supervision: An adult helps with cutting and taping, chooses the flying site, and supervises all flying.
safetyNotes: Never fly near power lines, roads, airports or in thunderstorms — if a kite catches on a power line, leave it and tell an adult to call the power company.
Fly in open spaces away from trees and other people.
